s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure against the $134B Databricks round priced by private investors in Feb 2026
did: Wrote Apache Spark as a Berkeley PhD student in 2009 as a faster in-memory replacement for Hadoop MapReduce, then in 2013 co-founded Databricks with six other Berkeley AMPLab people to sell a managed Spark service; he is CTO.
why: Spark was already the default engine inside enterprises before Databricks existed, because the AMPLab open-sourced it. The company sold the hosted version to buyers who had standardised on it for free, so distribution was won before the first invoice.
obst: Databricks had to survive the collapse of the Hadoop vendors that were its nearest comparables - Cloudera and Hortonworks merged in 2019 and were taken private in 2021 - while convincing investors that an open-source engine could carry a proprietary business.
turn: The 2017 pivot from selling Spark clusters to selling the lakehouse - unifying warehouse and data-lake workloads - which put Databricks in Snowflake's market instead of Cloudera's dying one.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; cross-checks against Samsara 8-K of 6 Jan 2026 putting Biswas and Bicket at 34.02% of shares
did: Co-founded Meraki out of an MIT mesh-networking project in 2006 and sold it to Cisco for $1.2B in 2012, then started Samsara in 2015 selling connected dashcams and sensors to trucking and construction fleets; IPO December 2021.
why: Both companies attacked industries where the incumbent hardware was sold once and never updated. Cloud-managed devices turned a one-time box sale into a subscription and let a small company out-iterate Cisco and Qualcomm-era telematics vendors.
obst: Meraki nearly died when Google, an early backer, launched competing municipal Wi-Fi and the founders had to buy out Google's stake; Samsara then faced a 2018 trade-secrets lawsuit from Cisco alleging the founders reused Meraki work.
turn: Cisco's $1.2B purchase of Meraki in November 2012, which gave the pair the capital and the credibility to attack a second, larger hardware market rather than take a corporate job.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure
did: Built Jerry and Davids Guide to the World Wide Web as a hand-curated link directory on a Stanford workstation in 1994, incorporated it as Yahoo in 1995, and stayed as Chief Yahoo through the 2016 sale of the core business to Verizon for $5B.
why: In 1994 search engines returned noise, so a human-edited directory was better than an algorithm. That head start bought the traffic that made Yahoo the default homepage, and the cash from it funded the 2005 Alibaba stake that ended up worth more than Yahoo itself.
obst: Yahoo lost search to Google after outsourcing it to them in 2000, rejected Microsofts $44.6B bid in 2008 and then watched its own market value fall below the value of its Asian holdings, an activist siege that ended in the company being broken up.
turn: The $1B investment in Alibaba in 2005, which converted a fading portal into a holding company whose Chinese stake dwarfed the operating business.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; wealth is a Gap Inc. family stake plus sports franchises
did: Youngest son of Gap founders Doris and Donald Fisher; runs the family investment vehicle Sansome Partners, sits on Gaps board, and owns the Oakland Athletics outright plus a controlling share of the San Jose Earthquakes.
why: The Fisher family kept a concentrated stake in Gap rather than diversifying out, and the stock compounded through the 1990s specialty-retail boom. Sports franchises then worked as a second concentrated bet with public subsidy attached.
obst: Gaps same-store sales fell for most of the 2010s and the family had to accept outside CEOs and store closures; the Athletics spent two decades failing to win a new Oakland ballpark before Fisher moved the club to Sacramento and then Las Vegas, drawing sustained fan boycotts.
turn: Buying the Athletics with Lew Wolff in 2005 for about $180M, a franchise later valued above $1B largely on relocation rights rather than on-field results.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure covering his Plaid stake and majority ownership of Column
did: Co-founded Plaid in 2012 with Zach Perret to sell an API that lets fintech apps read bank accounts, then in 2022 bought a chartered bank and rebuilt it as Column, a developer-facing bank he owns outright and which now banks Brex and Mercury.
why: Every consumer fintech needed bank-account access and none wanted to negotiate with 11,000 institutions. Plaid became the single integration point. Column went a layer deeper - owning the charter removes the sponsor bank that usually takes the margin and the veto.
obst: The Justice Department sued to block Visas $5.3B purchase of Plaid on antitrust grounds in November 2020 and the deal was abandoned in January 2021; Plaid also settled a $58M class action in 2021 over how much bank data it collected.
turn: The collapse of the Visa acquisition in January 2021 - Plaid then raised at $13.4B, four times what Visa had agreed to pay, and Hockey used the proceeds to self-fund a bank charter.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; Houston holds more than 20% of Dropbox
did: Started Dropbox in 2007 after forgetting a USB stick on a bus, demoing file sync as a screencast to get into Y Combinator; took it public on Nasdaq in 2018 and still runs it with more than 700 million registered users.
why: Sync had to be invisible to work, and the incumbents shipped it as a folder you had to think about. Dropbox made the file system itself the product and grew through a referral loop that paid in storage rather than cash, so acquisition cost was near zero.
obst: Steve Jobs told Houston in 2009 that Dropbox was a feature not a product and Apple shipped iCloud two years later; Google and Microsoft then bundled free storage, forcing Dropbox to pivot from consumer sync to paid business collaboration.
turn: The 2007 Hacker News screencast that produced 75,000 waitlist signups overnight and proved demand before the product could actually scale.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; roughly 4% of Coinbase plus a stake in Paradigm
did: Left Goldman Sachs FX trading to co-found Coinbase with Brian Armstrong in 2012 as a regulated place for ordinary Americans to buy bitcoin; left day-to-day in 2017 and co-founded the crypto fund Paradigm in 2018, now above $8B in assets.
why: Every other 2012 exchange treated compliance as an obstacle. Coinbase treated licences and bank relationships as the product, so when Mt. Gox and its successors collapsed, it was the only US venue institutions and regulators would touch.
obst: Coinbase spent years unable to keep a US banking partner, was sued by the SEC in June 2023 for operating an unregistered exchange, and survived two multi-year price collapses in which trading revenue fell by more than half.
turn: The 2017 retail mania, when Coinbase went from a niche wallet to the most-downloaded iPhone app in the US and its revenue crossed $1B, three years before the direct listing.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Forbes values each Cursor cofounder at about $2.4B in SpaceX shares received at the August 2026 close of the $60B acquisition
did: Co-founded Anysphere in 2022 with three MIT classmates and shipped Cursor, an AI code editor forked from VS Code; it passed $1B in annualised revenue before SpaceX bought the company for $60B in August 2026.
why: Rivals bolted AI onto an existing editor as an autocomplete plugin. Forking the editor itself let Cursor control the whole context window - which files the model sees and how edits are applied - so its suggestions landed where a plugin could only guess.
obst: Cursor was built on top of Microsofts VS Code and OpenAI and Anthropic models, so both its distribution surface and its core input were controlled by companies that shipped competing products; Microsoft restricted proprietary extensions to forks in 2025.
turn: The 2024 switch from selling completions to selling agentic multi-file edits, which took Cursor from a plugin substitute to the tool teams standardised on.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Forbes applies each cofounders roughly 22% stake to Mercors $10B October 2025 private valuation
did: Dropped out of Georgetown to start Mercor in 2023 with two school friends, first as AI-screened contract recruiting and then as the marketplace that supplies expert human labellers to AI labs; annualised revenue passed $500M by September 2025.
why: Frontier labs ran out of internet text and switched to paying doctors, lawyers and traders to write training data. Mercor already had the vetting pipeline and the contractor payments rails, so it captured a spend line that did not exist two years earlier.
obst: Scale AI sued Mercor in 2025 alleging a former employee took trade secrets, and the business depends on a handful of frontier labs that each have the scale to build the same data-labelling operation in house.
turn: The February 2025 Series B at $2B, when Mercor stopped describing itself as a recruiting startup and repriced as AI training-data infrastructure.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Forbes applies his founder stake to Perplexitys $20B 2025 private valuation
did: Left OpenAI research to co-found Perplexity in August 2022 with Andy Konwinski, Denis Yarats and Johnny Ho, building an answer engine that cites its sources instead of returning ten blue links.
why: Google could not put a direct answer above its own ads without cannibalising the ad unit that funds it. Perplexity had no such constraint, so it shipped the format Google could not, and citations gave it a defence publishers would tolerate longer than scraping.
obst: News Corp sued Perplexity in October 2024 for copying Dow Jones and New York Post content, Forbes and Wired accused it of plagiarising articles, and Amazon moved against its agentic shopping browser in 2025.
turn: The launch of Pages and the publisher revenue-sharing programme in 2024, which converted an adversarial relationship with media owners into a distribution deal.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; roughly 4% of DoorDash, public on the NYSE since December 2020
did: Co-founded DoorDash as a Stanford undergraduate in 2013 after the founders cold-called Palo Alto restaurants, wrote the original dispatch code, and is now head of consumer engineering at the company.
why: Grubhub and Seamless only took orders and left delivery to the restaurant, so they could only serve places that already had drivers. Owning the courier network opened suburbs and chains like Cheesecake Factory that had never delivered at all.
obst: DoorDash burned cash for years against better-funded rivals, was sued in 2019 over tip-skimming in its courier pay model and forced to change it, and faced California Proposition 22 and a wave of municipal fee caps during the pandemic.
turn: The 2018 SoftBank round and the decision to buy suburban share while Uber Eats defended cities, which flipped DoorDash to US market leader by 2019.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Forbes estimates he owns about 30% of Notion, last valued at $10B
did: Founded Notion in 2013 to let non-programmers assemble their own software from blocks; nearly ran out of money in 2015, moved the team to Kyoto to cut costs, rewrote the product and relaunched it in 2016.
why: Notion raised only about $330M across its life and stayed close to profitable, so Zhao kept roughly a third of the company where a normal SaaS founder would hold under 15%. Word-of-mouth growth through student and startup users replaced a sales force.
obst: The first version failed in 2015, the company laid off almost everyone and Zhao and Simon Last rebuilt it as two people in Japan; Notion was later blocked in China and had to defend against Atlassian and Microsoft bundling equivalents free.
turn: The 2018 launch of Notion 2.0, which added databases and templates and turned a note app into a workspace teams paid per seat for.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026; cross-checked to Figma DEF 14A of 22 Apr 2026 showing 54,388,280 Class B shares
m: Published Forbes figure; the proxy stake at the FIG close of $27.10 on 21 Aug 2026 implies $1.47B
did: Took a Thiel Fellowship to drop out of Brown in 2012 and built Figma with classmate Evan Wallace - a design tool that runs in the browser with multiple people editing one file; listed on the NYSE in July 2025.
why: Design files lived on individual laptops and were mailed around as versioned exports. Putting the canvas in WebGL in the browser made design multiplayer and, more importantly, made the file a link engineers and PMs could open without buying a licence.
obst: Figma shipped nothing for four years while Wallace fought browser rendering performance; Adobe then agreed to buy the company for $20B in 2022 and the deal was abandoned in December 2023 after UK and EU regulators moved to block it.
turn: The collapse of the Adobe deal in December 2023 - Figma took a $1B break fee, stayed independent and went public 19 months later.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time figure; about 7% of Maplebear plus options on 1% more
did: After twenty failed startup attempts he wrote the first version of Instacart in 2012 and got into Y Combinator late by ordering the partners a six-pack through his own app; the company listed on Nasdaq in 2023 as Maplebear.
why: Webvan had died building warehouses. Instacart owned no inventory and no trucks - it rented the shelves of Safeway and Costco and charged the shopper for time. Asset-light meant it could enter a city in weeks instead of years.
obst: Grocers who first partnered later launched competing delivery and Amazon bought Whole Foods in 2017; shopper-classification lawsuits and California Proposition 22 threatened the cost base, and the 2023 IPO priced far below the 2021 private mark of $39B.
turn: The 2017 decision to sell grocers their own white-label delivery and, later, retail media - turning a marketplace fee into a software and advertising business with real margin.

s: Okta DEF 14A filed 7 May 2026: 368,707 Class A and 6,512,134 Class B shares; OKTA closed at $135.14 on 21 Aug 2026
m: Proxy beneficial-ownership table times market price: 6,880,841 shares x $135.14 = $930M
did: Left his job running engineering at Salesforce in 2009 to co-found Okta with Frederic Kerrest, selling single sign-on as a cloud service; IPO 2017, still chairman and CEO.
why: Identity had been an on-premise directory owned by Microsoft. As companies bought dozens of separate SaaS tools, someone neutral had to hold the login, and a vendor that sold no applications of its own was the only party every application vendor would integrate with.
obst: Okta spent its first three years being told identity was a Microsoft feature; in January 2022 the Lapsus group breached a support contractor and Oktas delayed disclosure cost it customers, and a second support-system breach in October 2023 knocked roughly a fifth off the share price in a day.
turn: Winning large regulated enterprises after 2015 by proving Okta could sit in front of on-premise Active Directory rather than demanding it be replaced.

s: Reddit DEF 14A filed 23 Apr 2026: 1,868,737 Class A and 3,786,584 Class B shares; RDDT closed at $153.29 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 5,655,321 owned shares x $153.29 = $867M; excludes the 45.9M Class B shares he votes under proxy but does not own
did: Co-founded Reddit in 2005 with Alexis Ohanian in Y Combinators first batch, sold it to Conde Nast in 2006 for about $10M, left in 2009, then returned as CEO in 2015 and took the company public in March 2024.
why: The 2006 sale was tiny because Reddit had no revenue model; the money came from coming back. His 2021 grant was struck when Reddit was privately marked around $10B, and the 2024 IPO plus the AI-licensing deals that followed repriced user-generated text as training data.
obst: Reddit ran on volunteer moderators who twice revolted - over the 2015 firing of Victoria Taylor and over the June 2023 API pricing change that took thousands of subreddits dark days before the IPO filing - and the company had never posted an annual profit when it listed.
turn: The 2023 API repricing, which broke third-party apps and cost enormous goodwill but converted Reddits archive into paid licensing revenue from Google and OpenAI.

s: Figma DEF 14A filed 22 Apr 2026: Wu-Wallace Family Trust holds 26,730,324 Class B shares, 32.3% of the class; FIG closed at $27.10 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 26,730,324 shares x $27.10 = $724M; Field votes the shares under an irrevocable proxy but Wallace retains the economics
did: Co-founded Figma with Dylan Field in 2012 as its CTO and personally wrote the WebGL rendering engine that made browser-based vector editing fast enough to replace desktop tools; left the company in 2021 and later built the esbuild bundler.
why: The entire bet was that a browser could render a complex design canvas at 60 frames per second. Nobody else believed it, so nobody else tried, and the four years Wallace spent on the renderer became the moat that Sketch and Adobe never crossed.
obst: Figma had no shippable product for four years while the rendering engine was rebuilt against browsers that kept changing WebGL behaviour, and the team had to reverse-engineer font rasterisation because no browser exposed what designers needed.
turn: The 2015 internal demo of a live multiplayer canvas at usable speed, which proved the four-year engineering bet and unlocked the 2016 public launch.

s: Forbes profile reports a nearly 10% Dropbox stake; DBX market capitalisation was $7.50B at the 21 Aug 2026 close
m: Stake percentage last published by Forbes applied to current market cap; he has filed no Form 4 since April 2020, so later sales are unknown and the figure is a ceiling
did: Dropped out of MIT in 2007 to co-found Dropbox with Drew Houston and served as CTO until 2016, building the sync engine and the client that ran on Windows, Mac and Linux at a time when cross-platform sync barely worked.
why: Sync is a hard distributed-systems problem disguised as a folder. Ferdowsis engine handled conflict resolution and partial-file transfer well enough that users stopped noticing it, which is the only state in which a sync product wins.
obst: Dropbox had to defend a consumer business against three platform owners giving away the same storage; it also survived a 2012 credential-stuffing breach that exposed 68 million accounts and was only fully disclosed in 2016.
turn: The 2011 refusal of an acquisition approach from Apple, after which Dropbox raised at $4B and committed to building a standalone company.

s: HashiCorp DEFM14A filed 13 Jun 2024: 17,749,373 shares worth $621,228,055 plus $11.0M of options and $14.2M of RSUs at IBMs $35.00 cash price; deal closed 27 Feb 2025
m: Merger consideration table at $35.00 per share, about $646M gross before tax
did: Co-founded HashiCorp in 2012 with University of Washington classmate Mitchell Hashimoto, was CTO through the 2021 IPO, and sold the company to IBM for $6.4B in cash, closing February 2025.
why: HashiCorp gave away Terraform, Vault and Consul as open source until they became the default way infrastructure was described, then sold the enterprise controls. Cloud providers could not displace tools whose whole point was being neutral across AWS, Azure and Google.
obst: The August 2023 switch of Terraform from an open-source licence to the Business Source Licence triggered a community revolt and the OpenTofu fork backed by the Linux Foundation, and revenue growth slowed sharply before IBM bid.
turn: The 2017 release of Terraform Enterprise, which converted a widely used free tool into the paid control plane large companies actually needed.

s: SEC Form 4 filed 21 May 2026: 2,569,869 shares held directly and 503,052 through trusts; BE closed at $201.45 on 21 Aug 2026
did: Ran a NASA Mars project at the University of Arizona building a device to make oxygen from Martian air, then reversed it into a solid-oxide fuel cell and founded Bloom Energy in 2001 to sell on-site power boxes to companies; IPO 2018.
why: Bloom sells firm power to customers who cannot wait for a grid interconnection. When AI datacentres began queueing years for utility capacity after 2023, a generator that ships on a truck and runs on gas or hydrogen became the only fast option, and the order book repriced.
obst: Bloom burned more than $1B before revenue, depended on subsidies that repeatedly lapsed, was hit by a 2019 short-seller report alleging understated servicing costs and a restatement of managed-service accounting in 2020, and traded under $3 in 2020.
turn: The 2023-2025 datacentre power crunch, which turned Bloom from a subsidised clean-energy story into a supplier of scarce, immediately available electricity.

s: Forbes profile figure of $600M dated 3 Jun 2025
m: Published Forbes list figure; Forbes estimates she took about $765M in cash from the August 2022 Mondelez purchase of Clif Bar
did: Joined the business that became Clif Bar in 1984 and ran it as co-owner and co-CEO with her husband Gary Erickson, building an organic energy bar sold first to cyclists; they sold the company to Mondelez in August 2022 for about $2.9B.
why: Clif stayed employee-owned and refused the 2000 sale, which meant no private-equity owner ever stripped the brand. Owning the whole equity for thirty years, rather than a diluted slice, is why a mid-size food company produced a nine-figure personal outcome.
obst: In 2000 the pair walked away from a $120M signed sale to Quaker at the closing table, then had to borrow heavily to buy out the co-founder for about $65M, leaving the company loaded with debt in a category dominated by Nestle-owned PowerBar.
turn: Refusing the Quaker sale in 2000 and buying out the co-founder instead, which concentrated the equity that the 2022 Mondelez deal eventually paid out.

s: SEC Form 4 filed 12 Aug 2026: 1,245,679 shares in trust plus 31,440 in two childrens trusts; ISRG closed at $378.81 on 21 Aug 2026
did: Joined Intuitive Surgical in 1996 as a control systems analyst from SRI International, became CEO in 2010 and executive chair in 2025; the da Vinci robot went from an unproven device to more than 2.7 million procedures a year.
why: Intuitive sells the razor and the blades: a capital system plus per-procedure instruments that expire after a set number of uses. Surgeons trained on da Vinci will not retrain, so each installed system locks in a decade of consumable revenue.
obst: Intuitive faced a 2013 FDA safety review and a wave of product-liability suits over da Vinci complications that halved the stock, then defended antitrust suits from independent instrument repairers challenging the usage-limit chips at the core of its razor-blade model.
turn: Extending da Vinci beyond prostatectomy into hernia and colorectal surgery after 2012, which multiplied the addressable procedure count and restarted growth after the safety scare.

s: Forbes Americas Richest Self-Made Women, 3 Jun 2025: $440M
m: Published Forbes list figure struck against Vantas $2.45B mark; the company was marked at $4.15B in July 2025, so the figure predates that round
did: Left Union Square Ventures and Dropbox to found Vanta in 2018, automating the evidence collection behind SOC 2 and ISO 27001 audits so startups could get certified in weeks instead of a year.
why: Compliance was a consulting engagement priced by the hour. Vanta wired directly into AWS, Okta and the HR system and produced the evidence continuously, which turned an audit into a subscription and made the buyer the startup rather than the auditor.
obst: She wrote the first version herself without an engineering team, then had to convince audit firms - whose billable hours the product destroyed - to accept machine-generated evidence, while Drata raised aggressively behind her in the same category.
turn: Crossing $10M in annual recurring revenue in 2021 on almost no outside capital, which proved the category and let her raise at terms that kept her stake large.

s: SEC Form 4 filed 23 Jun 2026: 521,755 shares direct and 1,424,603 in trust; NVDA closed at $214.72 on 21 Aug 2026
did: Joined Nvidia in 2007 as executive vice president of operations after running operations at JDS Uniphase and Coherent; she owns the supply chain that turns TSMC wafers and HBM memory into shipped GPU systems.
why: Nvidias constraint since 2023 has not been demand or design but CoWoS packaging capacity and HBM supply. The operations seat is where allocation is fought for, and equity granted to that seat before 2018 compounded with the shortage it manages.
obst: She inherited the 2008 defective-packaging failure that forced Nvidia to take a $200M charge on faulty mobile GPUs, then had to hold supply through the 2018 crypto inventory glut, the 2020-2022 pandemic shortages and the export bans that stranded China-bound product.
turn: The 2022-2023 shift from selling chips to shipping whole DGX and HGX systems, which made operations - not silicon design alone - the binding constraint on Nvidias revenue.

s: SEC Form 4 filed 23 Jul 2026: 163,288 shares direct plus 1,792,478 held through the HJ Family Trust and six LLCs; CRM closed at $209.17 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,955,766 shares x $209.17 = $409M; excludes more than two decades of prior sales
did: Co-founded Salesforce with Marc Benioff in a San Francisco apartment in 1999 and wrote the first version of the CRM with two other engineers; still at the company as CTO of Slack after 27 years.
why: Siebel sold licences that took eighteen months to install. Salesforce ran one multi-tenant instance every customer shared, so a new customer cost almost nothing to add and upgrades shipped to everyone at once - the economics that made the subscription price possible.
obst: The founders were told repeatedly that enterprises would never put customer data on someone elses servers; a multi-day outage in December 2005 and a phishing breach in 2007 each revived that objection at the moment Salesforce was selling to large accounts.
turn: The 2007 launch of Force.com and the AppExchange, which turned a single application into a platform other vendors built on and made the customer base far harder to dislodge.

s: HashiCorp DEFM14A filed 13 Jun 2024: 10,986,794 Class B shares, 17.9% of the class; IBM paid $35.00 cash per share and closed the deal 27 Feb 2025
m: 10,986,794 shares x $35.00 = $385M gross before tax
did: Wrote Vagrant as a student side project in 2010, co-founded HashiCorp around it in 2012, and personally authored the first versions of Packer, Terraform, Consul, Vault and Nomad; left the company in December 2023, weeks before IBM bid.
why: He shipped six separate open-source tools that each became a category default before any of them had a price. By the time an enterprise wanted support, HashiCorp was already inside the build pipeline and the purchase order was a formality.
obst: Building a business on free software meant AWS, Azure and Google could each ship a native substitute; the August 2023 Business Source Licence change he had left the company partly over then split the Terraform community and produced the OpenTofu fork.
turn: Terraforms 2014 release, which replaced hand-written cloud provisioning scripts with declarative configuration and became the format the whole industry standardised on.

s: SEC Form 4 filed 12 Aug 2026: 1,995,934 shares in his revocable trust plus 35,000 in the Eltoukhy Foundation; GH closed at $170.69 on 21 Aug 2026
did: Sold his first sequencing company Avantome to Illumina in 2008, then co-founded Guardant Health in 2013 with AmirAli Talasaz to detect cancer from a blood draw rather than a tissue biopsy; the two run it as co-CEOs.
why: Liquid biopsy only works if you can find one tumour molecule among tens of thousands of normal ones. Guardant built the error-correction chemistry first and then spent years accumulating the outcome data that payers require, so reimbursement became the moat rather than the assay.
obst: Medicare coverage arrived only after years of evidence generation, Guardant lost a patent fight with Foundation Medicine, and its share price fell roughly 80% from the 2021 peak while the company burned cash proving its Shield colorectal screening test.
turn: FDA approval of Shield in July 2024 as the first blood test for primary colorectal cancer screening, which moved Guardant from treatment selection into population screening.

s: SEC Form 4 filed 2 Jun 2026: 2,565,489 shares in a revocable living trust plus 300,000 across two 2026 GRATs; CORT closed at $122.25 on 21 Aug 2026
did: A Stanford psychiatrist who co-founded Corcept in 1998 with colleague Alan Schatzberg to develop cortisol-blocking drugs; Korlym was approved for Cushings syndrome in 2012 and he has been CEO throughout.
why: Corcept picked a disease so rare that no large pharma would build a sales force for it, then priced and distributed the drug itself through a single specialty pharmacy. Owning distribution in an orphan indication is what let a company with one product fund its own pipeline without dilution.
obst: Corcept spent fourteen years pre-revenue, failed a depression trial that was its original thesis, then fought Teva through years of Hatch-Waxman litigation over generic mifepristone and absorbed a 2019 short-seller report attacking its single-pharmacy distribution.
turn: The February 2012 FDA approval of Korlym, which converted a two-decade research company into a cash-generating one and funded the relacorilant programme.

s: SEC Form 4 filed 23 Jul 2026: 3,554,034 shares direct plus 3,463,206 through a business limited partnership, a venture partnership, childrens trusts and a 401(k); BEN closed at $34.31 on 21 Aug 2026
did: Granddaughter of Franklin Resources founder Rupert Johnson Sr., she joined the firm in 1988, ran technology and then the retail business, and became CEO in 2020, the first woman to run the San Mateo asset manager.
why: The Johnson family still holds around 40% of Franklin, so an operating career inside the firm compounds a family stake rather than a salary. Buying Legg Mason in 2020 doubled assets under management at the moment active managers were losing shelf space to index funds.
obst: She took over weeks before the March 2020 crash while integrating the $4.5B Legg Mason acquisition, then absorbed sustained outflows and, in 2024, the SEC investigation and $37B of redemptions at Western Asset Management after its co-CIO was charged with cherry-picking trades.
turn: The July 2020 closing of the Legg Mason deal, which took Franklin from roughly $700B to about $1.4T in assets and bought scale in fixed income it could not grow organically.

s: SEC Form 4 filed 21 May 2026: 683,042 shares held in trust; PEN closed at $325.18 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 683,042 shares x $325.18 = $222M; excludes shares held directly and prior sales
did: A lawyer turned device entrepreneur who sold his first company Smart Therapeutics to Boston Scientific in 2004, then co-founded Penumbra in Alameda in 2004 to build catheters that vacuum blood clots out of the brain; IPO 2015.
why: Stroke thrombectomy was a procedure almost nobody performed because the tools were stent retrievers borrowed from cardiology. Penumbra built aspiration catheters specifically for cerebral vessels and simultaneously funded the trials that made the procedure standard of care.
obst: Penumbra had to recall its Jet 7 Xtra Flex catheter in December 2020 after reports of vessel damage and deaths, which triggered securities litigation and a short-seller campaign, and it later wrote off its Real immersive-therapy VR venture.
turn: The 2015 publication of the trials showing mechanical thrombectomy beat drugs for large-vessel stroke, which turned Penumbras catheters from a niche device into guideline-mandated equipment.

s: SEC Form 4 filed 17 Jul 2026: 888,524 shares direct and 33,877 in a managed account; WSM closed at $237.58 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 922,401 shares x $237.58 = $219M; excludes prior sales over a 31-year career
did: Joined Williams-Sonoma in 1995, built Pottery Barn Kids and then Pottery Barn Teen from nothing into billion-dollar brands, and has been CEO since 2010 running the group across Williams-Sonoma, West Elm and Rejuvenation.
why: She pushed the company to run e-commerce and catalogue as one in-house operation rather than outsourcing fulfilment, so Williams-Sonoma reached roughly two-thirds online sales while peers were still paying marketplace fees - and kept the gross margin that funded the buybacks.
obst: She took over in 2010 with the housing market still broken, then faced Amazon and Wayfair undercutting on price, a furniture supply chain wrecked by pandemic container costs, and a 2024 accounting restatement of freight-cost capitalisation that cost the shares in a single session.
turn: Launching West Elm and pushing it to a younger, lower-price customer through the 2010s, which gave the group growth that the mature Williams-Sonoma brand could not produce.

s: Okta DEF 14A filed 7 May 2026: 272,146 Class A and 1,089,931 Class B shares; OKTA closed at $135.14 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 1,362,077 shares x $135.14 = $184M; excludes sales since the 2017 IPO
did: Co-founded Okta with Todd McKinnon in 2009 after both worked at Salesforce, ran it as COO until 2023 and is now vice chairperson; he also founded Windproof Partners to invest in early-stage software.
why: Kerrest built the go-to-market that let a neutral identity vendor sell into IT departments already committed to Microsoft. Okta priced per-user across every application, so revenue grew with a customers SaaS sprawl without a new sales cycle.
obst: Okta was rejected by most investors in 2009 on the grounds that Microsoft owned identity; after the 2021 $6.5B Auth0 acquisition the sales organisations were merged badly, growth decelerated sharply and the 2022 Lapsus breach compounded the damage.
turn: The 2015 pivot to selling identity as the security perimeter rather than as convenience software, which reframed Okta as a security purchase with a security budget behind it.

s: SEC Form 4 filed 16 Jun 2026: 120,421 shares direct, 308,791 in a family trust and 14,500 through a partnership; SNPS closed at $397.87 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 443,712 shares x $397.87 = $177M; this is residual holdings only and excludes four decades of prior sales
did: Left General Electrics research lab in 1986 with a team and founded Synopsys around logic synthesis - software that compiles a chip description into gates; he was CEO until January 2024 and is executive chair.
why: Synthesis made it possible to design chips at a scale humans could not lay out by hand, so every advance in transistor count made the tool more necessary. Synopsys then bought its way across the flow until no serious chip could be taped out without touching its software.
obst: Synopsys fought a bitter multi-year patent and trade-secret war with Magma Design Automation from 2004, survived the 2001 and 2008 semiconductor downturns that cut customer design starts, and had to absorb dozens of acquisitions into one flow.
turn: The 1994 merger with Logic Modeling and the subsequent roll-up strategy, which turned a single-point synthesis tool into the end-to-end design platform that the industry now depends on.

did: Joined Coinbase in 2018 from LinkedIn, where she ran corporate development, and became president and COO; she has run more than thirty acquisitions for Coinbase including Xapo custody, Tagomi and Deribit.
why: Choi was hired to turn a retail brokerage into an institutional venue, and the acquisitions she ran bought the custody and derivatives pieces Coinbase could not build during a bear market - the segments that produced revenue when trading volumes collapsed.
obst: She joined months before the 2018 crypto winter and had to cut costs while integrating acquisitions, then managed operations through the June 2023 SEC lawsuit alleging Coinbase ran an unregistered exchange and the 2022 collapse of FTX and Celsius.
turn: The April 2021 direct listing, which repriced her 2018 equity grant and made Coinbase the first US crypto company on a national exchange.

s: SEC Form 4 filed 2 Jul 2026: 15,174 shares direct and 265,168 in the Ryan and Angela McInerney Trust; V closed at $371.04 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 280,342 shares x $371.04 = $104M; age 50 per the Visa DEF 14A of 8 Dec 2025
did: Ran consumer banking at JPMorgan Chase before joining Visa as president in 2013; became CEO in February 2023 and runs a network moving more than $16 trillion of payments volume a year.
why: Visa earns a toll on volume it does not underwrite and does not lend against, so the fortune here is pure equity compensation compounding on a business whose economics no operator can break. The job is defending the toll, not building the network.
obst: He inherited the collapse of Visas $5.3B Plaid acquisition to a DOJ antitrust suit, then faced the Justice Departments September 2024 monopolisation case over debit routing, the long-running interchange settlement litigation, and account-to-account rails built to bypass cards entirely.
turn: The 2016 integration of Visa Europe, which McInerney ran as president and which unified a fragmented European member-owned association into the global network.
